title: Air Rhodesia 827
summary: A Vickers Viscount registered VP-YND operating a scheduled civilian flight from Kariba to Salisbury, Rhodesia was shot down shortly after takeoff on 12 February 1979 by Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army (ZIPRA) guerrillas using a Strela 2 surface-to-air missile. The flight had been delayed and the pilots did not climb over a lake to get above the ceiling of shoulder-launched missiles before heading toward Salisbury. ZIPRA had information that Rhodesian Security Forces Commander General Peter Walls was on board and attempted to assassinate him, but he was on a second similar aircraft that escaped safely. All 59 passengers and crew on Flight 827 were killed. Following this incident, Air Rhodesia added shrouding to exhaust pipes and applied low-radiation paint as countermeasures against heat-seeking missiles.
probable_cause: The aircraft was struck by one or more Strela-2 missiles (Soviet-made surface-to-air missiles) fired by ZIPRA guerrillas during an attempted assassination of a military commander.

factors.evidence: ZIPRA had information that the Rhodesian Security Forces Commander General Peter Walls was on board, and they tried to assassinate him by firing a Strela-2 missile

events.text: Flight 827 took off from Kariba; the flight's departure had been delayed

The damaged aircraft came down in rough terrain in the Vuti African Purchase Area east of Lake Kariba; none of the 59 passengers or crew survived

title: Aeroflot 1691
summary: Flight 1691 took off at 19:32 local time after weather delay. Five seconds after liftoff, the left engine fire alarm sounded. The aircraft conducted four turns back towards Vnukovo, deflected flaps 20 degrees, then entered the glideslope. Two and a half seconds before impact, the crew moved throttles to takeoff thrust. The aircraft's left main landing gear struck cables on a road, then collided with ground 1,548 meters from the runway threshold. The board found the aircraft was overloaded and a mismatch of parts in the engine caused the false fire alarm.
probable_cause: The aircraft was overloaded. Other factors included lack of communication between crew and false fire alarm caused by mismatch of parts in the engine.

factors.evidence: The board found that the plane was overloaded
false fire alarm caused by a mismatch of parts in the engine
Other factors included the lack of communication between the crew

notes: Overload, false alarm from parts mismatch, and crew communication failure clearly identified; resulted in retirement of all Tu-104 aircraft from civil service

title: American Airlines 191
summary: American Airlines Flight 191, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 departing O'Hare for Los Angeles, crashed on 25 May 1979 after its left engine and pylon separated during takeoff rotation, killing all 271 aboard and 2 people on the ground in the deadliest US aviation accident. The NTSB found improper maintenance procedures had damaged the pylon, and that the separating engine severed hydraulic lines, causing an uncommanded retraction of the left wing's slats while also cutting power to the captain's instruments, stick shaker, and slat-disagreement warning system.
probable_cause: The NTSB found the probable cause was separation of the left engine and pylon assembly during takeoff, caused by damage from improper maintenance procedures, which led to asymmetric stall and loss of control after the slats retracted and stall-warning systems lost electrical power.

factors.evidence: The engine separation was attributed to damage to the pylon structure holding the engine to the wing, caused by improper maintenance procedures at American Airlines.
As the aircraft was beginning its takeoff rotation, engine number one separated from the left wing, flipping over the top of the wing and landing on the runway.
As the engine separated it severed hydraulic lines that lock the wing's leading-edge slats in place, and aerodynamic forces resulted in an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats.
The number-one electrical bus failed, causing several electrical systems to go offline, most notably the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat disagreement sensors.
The disrupted and unbalanced aerodynamics caused the aircraft to roll abruptly to the left until it was partially inverted, reaching a bank angle of 112 degrees, before crashing in an open field.

events.text: As the aircraft began its takeoff rotation from runway 32R, the number-one engine and its pylon assembly separated from the left wing and flipped over the top of the wing onto the runway.
The cockpit voice recorder lost power when the engine detached, capturing only a thump and the first officer exclaiming 'Damn!' before the recording ended.
The separating engine severed hydraulic lines that locked the left wing's leading-edge slats, and aerodynamic forces caused an uncommanded retraction of the outboard slats.
The number-one electrical bus failed with the engine, knocking out the captain's instruments, his stick shaker, and the slat-disagreement warning system.

With the damaged left wing producing far less lift than the right, the aircraft rolled abruptly to the left to a bank angle of 112 degrees before crashing in an open field by a trailer park near the runway.

title: 1979 Garuda Fokker F28 crash
summary: A 7-year-old Fokker F28 on approach to Medan struck Mount Sibayak at 5,560 feet with no survivors. The aircraft had been cleared for approach to runway 05 and asked to report passing the NDB beacon at 2,500 feet. The pilot initially reported maintaining 9,300 feet stating the NDB was unreliable, was instructed to maintain that height, but then reported 6,000 feet. The 7,200-foot volcano was struck at 5,560 feet, indicating a controlled descent below safe terrain clearance.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain during approach to Medan due to aircraft descending below safe altitude. Contributing factors included possible confusion over altitude reporting or reliability of navigation aids.

title: 1979 Dniprodzerzhynsk mid-air collision
summary: Two Aeroflot Tu-134As on intersecting airways converged over the Ukrainian SSR. The Kharkiv regional air traffic control center operated with high traffic density in a complex southwest sector with inadequate staffing. A 20-year-old 3rd-class controller under supervision of a 28-year-old 1st-class controller misheard a muffled transmission and failed to confirm that Flight 7880 acknowledged its altitude assignment, resulting in the aircraft remaining at the intersection altitude when the other aircraft descended to it.
probable_cause: Mistakes and violations by air traffic controllers who misheard transmissions and failed to properly confirm altitude clearances, resulting in aircraft converging at their navigation intersection.

title: Aeroflot 5484
summary: At cruise altitude of 9000 m, the flaps were extended without command at 00:24:35 at a speed of 530 km/h. The crew disengaged autopilot and attempted to level the aircraft by pulling the control column, but the aircraft entered a roll. When control column force was weakened at 00:24:52, the flaps extended fully to 30°, putting the aircraft in a steep dive exceeding maximum safe speed of 590 km/h. The inboard then outboard flaps tore off, causing a spin; at 3000 m altitude and 860 km/h speed the aircraft experienced 5g loading that tore off the left wing, and the fuselage broke apart in mid-air.
probable_cause: The flaps were extended at cruising altitude by unknown means; the crew's response and loss of control column authority during the subsequent dive prevented recovery. The flap control system design allowed accidental activation, and the design and placement of the switch were changed after the accident.

factors.evidence: Tests of the lock on the flap switch showed that accidentally activating it was indeed possible; the design and placement of the switch to release the flaps was changed after the accident to prevent accidental activation.
When force on the control column was weakened at 00:24:52 after the aircraft entered a roll, the flaps fully extended to 30° putting the aircraft in a steep dive.

At 00:25:13 MSK, the aircraft was at an altitude of 6000 m and flying at a speed of 660 km/h with a rate of descent of 36 m/s; the overload from the rate of descent may have limited the crew's capability to apply sufficient force on the control column.

The inboard flap tore off the right wing, followed by the outboard flaps tearing off; at 00:26 with the aircraft at 3000 m and 860 km/h the left wing tore off the airliner and the fuselage broke apart in mid-air.

The wreckage of the crash was found in the town of Inokovka on the floodplains of the Vorona River in Tambov Oblast, with the wreckage spread across an area 10750 by and all 63 passengers and crew killed.

events.text: At 00:23 MSK the flight contacted Penza air traffic control to report entering their airspace; that was the last time the flight made contact with controllers.
The flaps were extended for unknown reasons at 00:24:35 while the Tu-124 was at a speed of 530 km/h and flying at a heading of 65°; the crew immediately noticed the aircraft began to lose altitude.

Crew switched off the autopilot at 00:24:43; the flaps did not retract and the position led to quick descent; crew pulled on the control column to level the aircraft which briefly leveled before entering a roll.

At 00:26 MSK less than a minute after flap extension, the inboard and outboard flaps tore off the right wing causing a spin; at 3000 m altitude and 860 km/h speed with 5g loading the left wing tore off and the fuselage broke apart in mid-air.

title: Flight 2605 by Western Airlines
summary: Western Airlines Flight 2605 crashed while landing at Mexico City International Airport in dense fog after mistakenly landing on Runway 23L, which was closed for maintenance resurfacing. The controllers cleared the flight for an ILS approach to Runway 23L with an expected sidestep to open Runway 23R, but failed to use standard sidestep procedure phraseology. The crew, unaware of the sidestep requirement and seeing only ambiguous approach chart information for 23R, continued their descent on the ILS to closed Runway 23L. Visibility deteriorated to zero by the time of the crash.
probable_cause: Non-compliance with meteorological minimums for the approach procedure and failure to comply with aircraft operating procedures. The crew landed on Runway 23L which was closed for maintenance instead of the open Runway 23R. The ATC communication failed to clearly convey the sidestep procedure requirement, and the approach chart for 23R lacked published visual representation of the sidestep procedure.

title: PIA 740
summary: A Boeing 707 en route from Kano to Karachi via Jeddah was struck by fire in the aft section at 18 minutes after departure. The crew reported the fire to ATC and requested clearance to return to Jeddah. Due to rapidly spreading fire and smoke incapacitating the crew, the aircraft lost control and crashed into terrain near Taif, killing all 156 occupants.
probable_cause: In-flight fire of undetermined origin, likely caused by leaking gasoline or kerosene stoves carried by pilgrim passengers, ignited by spark or cigarette.

title: Air New Zealand 901

agencies.name: Royal Commission of Inquiry (Justice Peter Mahon)

summary: Air New Zealand Flight 901, a DC-10 on a scheduled Antarctic sightseeing flight from Auckland, flew into Mount Erebus on Ross Island on 28 November 1979, killing all 237 passengers and 20 crew. A Royal Commission found the cause was an uncoordinated overnight correction to the flight's computerized waypoint coordinates that rerouted the aircraft toward Mount Erebus without the crew being told, compounded by a sector whiteout that made the volcano's slope look like the flat Ross Ice Shelf.
probable_cause: The Royal Commission of Inquiry, led by Justice Peter Mahon, found the accident was primarily caused by an automatic correction to the flight path coordinates the night before, coupled with a failure to inform the flight crew, so the aircraft was rerouted toward Mount Erebus instead of down McMurdo Sound as the crew had been led to believe.

factors.evidence: an automatic correction made to the coordinates of the flight path the night before... coupled with a failure to inform the flight crew of the change
instead of being directed by computer down McMurdo Sound (as the crew had been led to believe), was instead rerouted to a path toward Mount Erebus
a layer of clouds blended with the white snow-covered volcano, forming a sector whiteout... deceived everyone on the flight deck
flew into Mount Erebus on Ross Island, Antarctica, killing all 237 passengers and 20 crew on board

events.text: Around 1:40 am on the morning of the flight, Air New Zealand's navigation section changed the McMurdo waypoint coordinate in the ground computer to align with the McMurdo TACAN beacon.
Flight 901 left Auckland International Airport at 8:00 am, scheduled to return to Christchurch at 7:00 pm after a sightseeing flight over Antarctica.
Captain Collins told McMurdo Station he would be dropping to 2000 ft and switched control of the aircraft to the autopilot.
A layer of cloud blended with the snow-covered volcano to form a sector whiteout, deceiving the flight deck into believing the mountainside was the Ross Ice Shelf.
The aircraft flew into Mount Erebus on Ross Island, Antarctica, killing all 237 passengers and 20 crew aboard.

notes: an initial investigation blamed pilot error, but the record follows the Royal Commission's finding as the text presents it as the concluded cause
